newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spanish economy churns out good news.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spanish economy churns out good news.

text.p: Spaniards showed exuberant confidence in their economy in three different surveys published on Wednesday, while official data confirmed falling unemployment and the government forecast further growth.
Business leaders surveyed for the first time by Spain's Association of Business Consultants gave high marks to the economy and showed increased optimism about future investment.
"It shows me that an improvement in outlook has taken place in Spain," Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro told journalists at the presentation of the survey in Madrid.
"The outlook has changed and today it's showing itself to be clearly positive."
The survey looked at a random sample of 405 top executives selected from 50,000 companies between March and June this year.

It found that 97 percent believed declining interest rates were positive for the economy, while 93 percent approved of falling inflation. A smaller majority, 64 percent, thought the shrinking public deficit was good news.
The study also showed that the business community were optimistic about prospects for the economy in the next six months, with 79 percent anticipating a rise in employment.
Earlier on Wednesday, Spain's National Statistics Institute said unemployment fell to 20.94 percent in the second quarter from 21.29 percent in the first, based on a household survey.
Montoro said the fall in Spain's stubbornly high jobless rate showed that growth was boosting employment.
"The numbers confirm that economic growth is really translating into the creation of employment," he said.

The business leaders were positive on five policies of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's conservative government: privatisations, control of public spending, structural reforms, labour market reform and employment.
But they said that in order to spur further economic development, the government should give a higher priority to labour market reform, jobs and public spending controls.

A separate study by business group CEOE said Spain's economic recovery in the past year was due both to government policy as well as company efforts to clean up balance sheets and streamline production.

The report said businesses had been able to create an average growth of 6.4 percent in capital goods investment while the government had managed to bring both price pressures and the public deficit under control.
"As a result, interest rates have been reduced, the peseta stabilised and financial markets have maintained an upward trend," the CEOE report concluded.
Spain's Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said on Wednesday the 1998 budget, expected in preliminary form on Friday, would show the pace of economic growth was being maintained.

"The budget for 1998 should consolidate the economic recovery and guarantee macroeconomic stability," Rato told journalists after meeting unions on the budget. There would be room for further interest rate cuts, he said.
Montoro also said the increasing competitiveness of Spanish companies and growth in output would not overheat the economy.
"This survey of business views confirms that this growth, in other words, this increase in sales, is in a manner that is compatible with a drop in inflation," he said.
Seventy-seven percent of business leaders in the CEOE report said sales rose in the past six months and would continue to do so.

A third opinion poll by the government's CIS institute showed on Wednesday that Spanish confidence in the economy had risen by almost 13 points since Aznar's Popular Party came to power in May 1996. Nearly 30 percent saw it improving in the upcoming year, while about nine percent said the economy would worsen.
"These data do nothing but confirm the growing confidence in the future of the Spanish economy," CIS said.
